title: Did Paul Invent Jesus's Divinity?

keyTerms.d: Paul “delivered” (Greek paredōka) what he “received” (parelabon) — the precise idiom used in Judaism for the transmission of authoritative tradition, the equivalent of the rabbinic masar and qibbel. He is not narrating his own experience; he is handing on something handed to him.

Across a decade and more of letters written to scattered churches to settle other questions, Paul never sets out to prove that Christ is divine. He everywhere assumes it, and a thing presupposed offhandedly by a writer making some other point was not up for debate — the startlingly high Christology is everywhere presupposed, never argued.

An Aramaic prayer left untranslated in Paul’s Greek-speaking churches: “Our Lord, come!” That the invocation survives in Aramaic is the point. It carries us back behind Paul’s Greek to the Aramaic-speaking Judean church — the very first community, already calling on the risen Jesus as the Lord who will come.

What most scholars regard as a pre-Pauline hymn describes one who was “in the form of God” and did not count “equality with God” a thing to be grasped, who took “the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men,” and is given “the name that is above every name.” The pre-Pauline dating is itself debated — Gordon Fee argues Paul composed it — but composed or quoted, the conviction it expresses is not one Paul argues into being.

When Paul reaches for language to describe the exalted Jesus, he does not reach outward to the mystery cults; he reaches into the Old Testament’s most jealously monotheistic texts — Isaiah 45, Joel 2:32 — and applies to Jesus the words reserved for Yahweh alone. The matrix is Jewish monotheism, not Hellenistic syncretism.

keyTerms.t: Inside the identity of the one God
keyTerms.d: Richard Bauckham’s framing: Jesus is placed on the Creator’s side of the line that Jewish monotheism drew between God and everything else — inclusion within the unique identity of the one God of Israel, not a second god. It is a widely influential framing, though the divine-identity category is itself debated (Larry Hurtado read the same data as a pattern of devotion; James F. McGrath disputes the category).

keyTerms.t: Israel’s confession, its two divine titles divided
keyTerms.d: In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul takes Israel’s own confession that the LORD is one and divides its two divine titles, so that the “one God” is the Father and the “one Lord” is Jesus Christ, “through whom are all things.” That reading is influential and genuinely contested: James F. McGrath argues that “one Lord” is set alongside the creed rather than folded into it. The point is inclusion of Jesus within the identity of the one God, not the importing of a second god.

The fourth- and fifth-century language of “one essence” and “two natures” came later — the church’s articulation of what was already in the texts, not a first-century phrase. Not that the deity of Christ was a later human invention: the words for it were refined over centuries; the reality is bedrock, there in the earliest layer we can reach.

derive.q: Paul introduces the creed with “I delivered to you … what I also received” — the technical idiom for handing on tradition — so the confession is…?
derive.ans: handed on to him, not composed by him
derive.why: The verbs are the precise idiom used in Judaism for the transmission of authoritative tradition. He is not narrating his own experience; he is handing on something handed to him — and the formula must predate his own receipt of it, which places its origin no later than the mid-to-late 30s — and within roughly two to five years of the crucifixion if he already had it at his conversion.

derive.q: In letters written to settle other questions, Paul never sets out to prove Christ is divine — he simply assumes it — so the divinity was…?
derive.why: A thing presupposed offhandedly by a writer making some other point was not up for debate. Colossians’ own authorship is debated; but the same presupposing-not-arguing pattern runs through the undisputed letters — Philippians, 1 Corinthians, Romans — so the observation does not stand or fall with it.

derive.q: A prayer to the risen Jesus survives untranslated, in Aramaic, inside Paul’s Greek letters — so the devotion…?
derive.ans: reaches behind Paul to the first Judean church
derive.why: That the invocation survives in Aramaic is the point. It carries us back behind Paul’s Greek to the Aramaic-speaking Judean church — the very first community, already calling on the risen Jesus as the Lord who will come. The highest devotion is not a late overlay Paul introduced; it is bedrock beneath him.

derive.q: To describe the exalted Jesus, Paul quotes Isaiah 45 — where to the LORD alone every knee shall bow — and Joel’s “call on the name of the LORD” — so the source of his language is…?
derive.ans: Jewish monotheism, not the pagan cults
derive.why: A man importing a second god from the mystery religions does not reach for the chapter of Isaiah that most insists there is no god beside the LORD. The matrix is Jewish monotheism, not Hellenistic syncretism — which is why the older derivation-from-paganism model has largely collapsed under closer study.

derive.q: The supposed inventor had violently persecuted the church for this very belief — so the inventor thesis…?
derive.why: A movement’s enemies do not usually defect to it, at ruinous personal cost, on the strength of nothing. You do not invent, at the cost of your standing and your safety and your inherited convictions, the very belief you had been trying to stamp out — a belief whose divine shape, as the Aramaic Marana tha and the hymn behind Philippians show, already reached back behind him.

derive.q: Grant all of it: Paul received the divine confession rather than inventing it. Does that, by itself, prove the confession true?
derive.ans: no — it shows the claim was made, not that it is correct
derive.why: That Paul handed on the belief that Jesus is the risen Lord establishes that the claim was made — at the movement’s foundation, by a formerly hostile witness — not that the claim is correct. Whether it is correct is the work of the resurrection evidence and of Jesus’s own words.

honestState.p1: The facts the inventor thesis starts from are not in dispute: the oldest datable Christian documents we possess are the letters of Paul, generally dated to the 50s — earlier than any of the Gospels; Paul did not walk with the earthly Jesus; and his Christology really is very high. The question is whether Paul originated that Christology, or inherited and expressed it. Several supports are debated and are carried with their limits: the pre-Pauline dating of the Philippians hymn (Gordon Fee argues Paul composed it), the authorship of Colossians, the divine-identity category (Hurtado read the same data as a pattern of devotion; James F. McGrath disputes it), and the reading of 1 Corinthians 8:6, which is influential and genuinely contested.
honestState.fairness: The disagreement with the developmental thesis is not really about dates — Ehrman himself finds a pre-existent Christ in material older than Paul’s letters — but about what kind of being the earliest Christians took Jesus to be: on his view what developed was the divine figure’s rank, not the date of pre-existence itself. And the dating witnesses are cited for the dating only: Lüdemann affirms the early date while rejecting a bodily resurrection; Dunn wrote as a mainstream critical historian, not an apologist.
honestState.verdict: So the honest answer to the question is no. Paul did not invent Jesus’s divinity. He is the single most important early witness to it — but a witness is precisely what he is: a man who received a confession, assumed it rather than argued it, clothed it in Israel’s own language for God, and embraced it only after it had overturned everything he believed. And this is what we hold to be true: the one Paul confessed as Lord is the eternal Son, fully God and fully man. This argument does not prove that; it clears the charge against it — the positive case rests on the resurrection and on Jesus’s own words.

order: Paul received the core confession rather than composing it.
He presupposes the divinity, applies Yahweh’s own texts to Jesus, and had been the confession’s persecutor.
Therefore Paul did not invent Jesus’s divinity — he received it.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its honest limit.
cards.a: Paul received the core confession rather than composing it — “I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received” (1 Corinthians 15:3). Limit: that Paul handed on the belief establishes that the claim was made — at the movement’s foundation, by a formerly hostile witness — not that the claim is correct. The received creed of 1 Corinthians 15 is about the resurrection; turn to the divinity itself, and the same pattern holds.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its honest limit.
cards.a: When Paul describes the exalted Jesus he applies Yahweh’s own exclusive texts to him (Isaiah 45 in Philippians 2; Joel 2:32 in Romans 10) — including Jesus within the identity of the one God, not importing a second god; and he had been the confession’s persecutor. Limit: the divine-identity framing is widely influential, though the category is itself debated.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That Paul did not invent Jesus’s divinity: the divine confession stands behind Paul, not with him. It does not by itself prove the confession true; whether it is correct is the work of the resurrection evidence and of Jesus’s own words.

cards.q: Why do “delivered” and “received” matter — and how old is what Paul received?
cards.a: They are the precise idiom used in Judaism for the transmission of authoritative tradition: he is handing on something handed to him. Reckoned backward from the fixed points of his biography, the formula must predate his own receipt of it — within roughly two to five years of the crucifixion, a date held across the spectrum.

cards.q: Why is “presupposed, never argued” stronger evidence than an argument would be?
cards.a: Because a thing presupposed offhandedly by a writer making some other point was not up for debate. Paul writes to settle other questions — a collection, a quarrel, a word of comfort — and assumes Christ’s divine status as common ground. The pattern runs through the undisputed letters, so it does not stand or fall with Colossians.

cards.q: What does a prayer surviving untranslated in Aramaic show?
cards.a: It carries us back behind Paul’s Greek to the Aramaic-speaking Judean church — the very first community, already calling on the risen Jesus as the Lord who will come (“Our Lord, come!”). The highest devotion is not a late overlay Paul introduced; it is bedrock beneath him.

cards.q: What does the Philippians hymn say of Christ — and what if Paul composed it himself?
cards.a: One who was “in the form of God” and did not count “equality with God” a thing to be grasped, who took “the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men,” and is given “the name that is above every name.” Its pre-Pauline dating is debated, but composed or quoted, the conviction it expresses is not one Paul argues into being.

cards.q: What is the “problem of direction” for the pagan-borrowing thesis?
cards.a: Paul does not reach outward to the mystery cults; he reaches into the Old Testament’s most jealously monotheistic texts and applies to Jesus the words reserved for Yahweh alone. A man importing a second god does not reach for the chapter that most insists there is no god beside the LORD.

cards.q: What does Paul do with Israel’s confession in 1 Corinthians 8:6 — and how secure is that reading?
cards.a: He divides its two divine titles: the “one God” is the Father and the “one Lord” is Jesus Christ, “through whom are all things.” Read as folded into the creed, it is not one more step up a ladder: no Jewish writer we know of wrote a second figure into the creed of divine uniqueness itself (Philo’s “second god,” the Logos, is the nearest case, and it is never placed inside that confession). The reading is influential and genuinely contested — some argue “one Lord” is set alongside the creed rather than folded into it.

cards.q: On the developmental thesis, what developed — so what is the real disagreement?
cards.a: On that view, what developed was the divine figure’s rank, not the date of pre-existence: the thesis itself finds a pre-existent Christ in material older than Paul, though it holds he was first conceived as a subordinate divine being. So the disagreement is not really about dates but about what kind of being the earliest Christians took Jesus to be — and there 1 Corinthians 8:6 and the Yahweh texts applied to Jesus speak. Read as folded into the creed, 1 Corinthians 8:6 is not one more step up a ladder; the words were refined over centuries; the reality is there in the earliest layer we can reach.

cards.q: Why is the persecutor the inventor thesis’s hardest witness?
cards.a: Because the reversal puts the causation backwards. He had violently persecuted the church for this belief — a crucified Messiah was a scandal, a hanged man under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23). You do not invent, at the cost of everything, the very belief you had been trying to stamp out. He did not build the confession; he joined it.

cards.q: What came later — and what did not?
cards.a: The developed creedal vocabulary — “one essence,” “two natures” — came later, as the church’s articulation of what was already in the texts. Not the deity of Christ, which was no later human invention: the words were refined over centuries; the reality is there in the earliest layer we can reach.

obj.q: Christianity is the religion Paul built about Jesus, not the religion of Jesus. Paul is the earliest writer, he never met Jesus, and his Christology is sky-high — he is the one who turned a Galilean preacher into a divine Lord.
obj.model: Grant what is true: Paul’s letters are the oldest datable Christian documents, he did not walk with the earthly Jesus, and his Christology really is very high. But he tells us he received the core confession rather than composing it — “I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received” (1 Corinthians 15:3) — and the material he carries reaches behind him: the Aramaic Marana tha, a prayer of the first Judean church, and the Philippians hymn (most take him to be quoting older material; composed or quoted, the conviction is not one he argues into being). When he describes the exalted Jesus he reaches for the Old Testament’s own words for Yahweh. And he had been the church’s violent persecutor: you do not invent, at the cost of everything, the very belief you had been trying to stamp out. He is a witness to the divine confession, not its author.

obj.q: Calling Jesus Kyrios, “Lord,” and worshipping him looks like the lords of the Hellenistic mystery cults. Paul, at home in the Greek world, imported that pattern into a Jewish sect.
obj.model: Here the derivation-from-paganism thesis meets its hardest problem, and it is a problem of direction. Paul applies to Jesus the climax of Isaiah 45, where the LORD swears that to him alone every knee shall bow — one of the most fiercely monotheistic passages in all of Scripture — and clinches Romans 10 with Joel’s “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved,” where the Lord one calls upon is Yahweh himself. A man importing a second god from the mystery religions does not reach for the chapter of Isaiah that most insists there is no god beside the LORD. The matrix is Jewish monotheism, not Hellenistic syncretism — which is why the older derivation-from-paganism model has largely collapsed. And as Martin Hengel argued, more happened in Christology in the less than two decades between the crucifixion and Paul’s letters than in the seven centuries that followed: the timeline is too fast, and the vocabulary too Jewish, for a slow drift out of paganism.

obj.q: Paul himself says his gospel was “not man’s gospel” but came “through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1:11–12). By his own account it came from him, not from anyone before him.
obj.model: That is the text the inventor thesis leans on hardest. But what Paul says came by revelation is his encounter with the risen Son and his commission to the Gentiles (Galatians 1:15–16), not a creed of his own devising. The confession itself he says he “received” (1 Corinthians 15:3), and the message he preached was set before the leading men of the Jerusalem church, those who had known Jesus, and was endorsed by them rather than corrected (Galatians 2:2, 6, 9). Three years after his conversion he stayed fifteen days with Cephas, the first name in the creed (Galatians 1:18).

obj.q: The earliest followers held an exaltation Christology. Even the pre-existent Christ found before Paul was a subordinate divine being — God’s chief angel, or a divinity of a lesser order. His elevation to the co-equal God is the later step, and Paul stands near the head of that trajectory.
obj.model: Notice what that concedes: the disagreement is not really about dates — this view itself finds a pre-existent Christ in material older than Paul’s letters — but about what kind of being the earliest Christians took Jesus to be. In 1 Corinthians 8:6 Paul takes Israel’s own confession that the LORD is one and divides its two divine titles: the “one God” is the Father and the “one Lord” is Jesus Christ, “through whom are all things.” That reading is genuinely contested — James F. McGrath argues “one Lord” is set alongside the creed rather than folded into it — but read as folded into the creed, it is not one more step up a ladder. Wisdom is praised; Enoch is exalted; but no Jewish writer we know of wrote a second figure into the creed of divine uniqueness itself (Philo’s “second god,” the Logos, is the nearest case, and it is never placed inside that confession). Paul did. On Bauckham’s reading — widely influential, though the category is debated — the earliest Christians expressed the highest possible claim, inclusion in the divine identity, from the start. The words for it were refined over centuries; the reality is there in the earliest layer we can reach, and Paul stands inside that layer, not above it.

unseen.q: Those other Pauline lines don’t make Jesus God. “Sin against Christ,” “test Christ,” a prayer-wish addressed to the Father and Jesus together — on the agent reading, that is simply the language of God’s agent, the one who acts for God, not God himself.
unseen.model: On its own, “sin against Christ” (1 Corinthians 8:12) proves little — but it belongs to a pattern. Two chapters later, retelling Israel’s rebellion in the wilderness, Paul warns the Corinthians not to “test Christ, as some of them did” (10:9; the earliest manuscript reads “Christ,” some read “the Lord”), and asks, “Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?” (10:22) — the Lord whose cup and table they share (10:21), in the language of Deuteronomy 32, where it is the LORD whom Israel provokes to jealousy with foreign gods. And in his earliest surviving letter he asks the Father and Jesus together, with a single verb, to act: “May our God and Father Himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you” (1 Thessalonians 3:11). On the agent reading these would be the language of God’s agent; but the jealousy Israel provoked was the LORD’s alone, and Jewish piety characteristically did not address prayer, or prayer-wishes like this one, to an agent. And whatever room Judaism had for exalted intermediaries, the angels among them characteristically refuse worship and redirect it to God, while the earliest Christians were praying to Jesus and singing hymns about him within the first two decades. So these lines do not fit the agent reading: as Bauckham puts it, the earliest Christians expressed the highest possible claim — inclusion in the divine identity — from the start, using the very resources of Jewish monotheism. The words for it were refined over centuries; the reality is bedrock, and it is there in the earliest layer we can reach. Paul stands inside that layer, not above it.
